sources.article: CIAD-2026-0046 Threat Actors Exploiting Payment and Disbursement APIs for Unauthorized Fund Transfers in BFSI Entities Original Issue Date: October 09, 2026 Severity Rating: Critical Description CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin has observed multiple cyber attack campaigns targeting non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers and wallet operators. Threat actors compromise internet-facing applications, exposed APIs and privileged endpoints, steal payment aggregator/gateway and partner-bank API credentials, and invoke disbursal/fund-transfer APIs directly from within the entities' own whitelisted infrastructure, completely bypassing application-level controls such as loan creation, KYC, sanction, beneficiary verification, balance sufficiency and per-transaction limits. The fraudulent transactions carry dummy reference identifiers, exceed per-transaction limits, and credit funds to attacker-controlled mule accounts across multiple banks. Analysis of these attacks further indicates the possible use of AI-assisted offensive tooling, with the interval between initial compromise and fraudulent fund transfer reducing significantly in recent incidents. Attacker IPs are predominantly associated with hosting infrastructure. Attack Vector Initial compromise is achieved through: Exploitation of exposed internet-facing applications and application server middleware vulnerabilities. Abuse of deprecated, unauthenticated or unused APIs with unrestricted file-upload functionality. Use of stolen long-lived static API tokens hard-coded in source code. Supply-chain compromise of source-code repositories via forged commits. Exploitation of plaintext credentials in configuration files, source code or databases. Access to applications and remote services lacking MFA. Post-compromise, attackers establish persistence via web shells and backdoors, conduct reconnaissance of payment databases and API integrations, steal payment aggregator/gateway and bank API credentials, and directly invoke disbursal/fund-transfer APIs to execute unauthorized transactions. Key TTPs Observed Direct invocation of disbursal/fund-transfer APIs from whitelisted infrastructure using valid credentials. Bypassing of application-level checks (KYC, sanction, beneficiary verification, balance sufficiency). Supply of dummy loan/transaction reference numbers with no corresponding records. Rapid execution of multiple high-value transactions through IMPS/NEFT rails. Transfer of funds to mule accounts across multiple banks with immediate withdrawal. Deletion/truncation of logs, tampering with EDR tools, and anti-forensic cleanup. Possible use of AI-assisted offensive frameworks and large numbers of custom scripts. Recommended Actions Enforce MFA for payment platforms, administrative portals, payment/bank APIs and remote access services. Maintain a complete API inventory; formally decommission deprecated and unused APIs. Enforce per-session authentication on all APIs; eliminate long-lived static tokens. Bind multi-stage transaction flows cryptographically so debit-stage APIs cannot be invoked without preceding validation stages. Implement maker-checker or second-level verification for all fund movement. Validate every payout against sanctioned/approved records; reject reference identifiers with no corresponding records. Enforce per-transaction and per-day cumulative ceilings at the API/payment stage. Apply beneficiary validation (penny-drop, name-to-account matching) and velocity limits on all disbursement paths. Restrict outbound (egress) traffic from production servers through allow-listing. Store all API keys and credentials in secure secret management solutions or HSMs; enforce rotation. Implement real-time monitoring of fund transfers with velocity, amount-band and new-beneficiary checks, with automated blocking or holding. Enable near-real-time reconciliation of system records with bank/aggregator statements. Maintain centralized logging and log retention of at least 180 days. Deploy EDR with tamper protection on servers and endpoints. Adopt behavioural anti-automation controls (rate limiting, sequence-binding) to disrupt script-driven API abuse. Remove internet exposure of internal applications; enforce geofencing under formal change control. Isolate development, testing and production environments. Conduct regular VA/PT including API security testing. Upon detection of suspicious activity: disable compromised accounts, suspend affected APIs, preserve forensic evidence, rotate all credentials, and report to CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin at incident@cert-in.org.in. Reporting Entities are advised to report any signs of suspicious activity related to this attack campaign to CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin at incident@cert-in.org.in , along with all relevant logs, at the earliest.
sources.limitations: Reported Indian financial-sector campaign. Recommendations are not measured effectiveness.

sources.article: CIAD-2026-0058 Escalation of AI-Driven Attacks on BFSI Entities by Threat Actor "CRAFTY FALCON" Original Issue Date: November 04, 2026 Severity Rating: Critical Overview This advisory is an update to CERT-In Advisory CIAD-2026-0046 dated 09 October 2026 on Threat Actors Exploiting Payment and Disbursement APIs for Unauthorized Fund Transfers in BFSI Entities. Continued analysis of incidents reported by affected entities including non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment aggregators, payment service providers and cryptocurrency exchanges / virtual digital asset service providers has revealed a significant escalation of this campaign. Computer Security Incident Response Team - Finance (CSIRT-Fin) under CERT-In has designated the threat actor responsible for this campaign as "CRAFTY FALCON": an AI-assisted financial threat actor that surveys its targets with machine intelligence, operates at machine speed and strikes by invoking the victim's own payment and disbursement APIs. The threat is active and ongoing. CSIRT-Fin continues to receive reports of successful attacks, including from NBFCs and fintech entities that had already received the earlier restricted (TLP:AMBER) advisories and had undertaken remediation. The same entities have been deliberately re-targeted, including after incomplete remediation and attacks have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response. All BFSI entities are strongly advised to treat this campaign as an immediate and continuing threat. Analysis has identified the use of multiple publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools against affected entities including the "ARTEX" family of LLM-based, "PentAGI" autonomous multi-agent AI penetration testing system and the "Cairn" attack search engine, in addition to the "CyberStrikeAI" framework. These tools execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession and adapt their payloads based on target responses. The supporting attack infrastructure rotates IP addresses within hours to days; infrastructure fingerprints and detailed detection rules have been shared with entities through the restricted advisories. Description Analysis of the reported incidents indicates below attack pattern: Cloud infrastructure of entities targeted including compute, serverless and management services with cloud management services (such as AWS Systems Manager and Lambda) abused to execute commands and deploy malicious files, blending malicious activity into legitimate cloud management channels. Internet-exposed non-production environments (UAT/staging/testing) used as entry points, followed by movement to production environments using shared credentials, tokens or network paths. Application codebases reverse-engineered by the threat actor to develop tailored exploits; unauthorized API calls subsequently initiated using altered/modified application packages, defeating controls that assumed only the legitimate client application would call the APIs. IP allow-listing bypassed by originating traffic from whitelisted third-party fetcher IP pools (such as content-acceleration and app-store review fetchers); any Internet user can cause such shared fetcher services to fetch arbitrary URLs. Micro-value test transactions (such as Rs. 1) performed to validate unauthorized fund flows before executing large-value transfers. Merchant settlement APIs of payment aggregators exploited or abused to move funds. Newly published vulnerabilities exploited as soon as they become public, including file-upload and deserialization exploit chains leading to web shells in PHP and Node.js applications. Cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual digital asset service providers targeted, with wallet keys stolen and funds siphoned from cryptocurrency wallets. Large numbers of custom, tailored scripts created on the fly, with functionally identical variants refined in rapid succession; a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development. Recommended Actions Treat this campaign as active and escalating: maintain heightened 24x7 security monitoring, with increased staffing and lowered alert thresholds during holidays, weekends and other low-coverage windows. After any incident, assume persistence: perform full eradication with forensic verification and continue periodic threat hunting; entities have been re-attacked after incomplete remediation. Enable centralized, real-time monitoring of cloud audit logs with alerting on high-risk events such as remote command execution, serverless function code updates and creation of roles, users or access keys. Restrict cloud management and serverless execution to approved principals and accounts; alert on any interactive remote-management session or serverless function code change in production. Enforce instance metadata service protections and least-privilege roles for instances and functions; deny wildcard egress in security groups; configure serverless functions with no Internet egress by default. Isolate UAT/staging/testing environments from production - no shared credentials, tokens, API keys, databases or direct network paths and apply production-grade hardening and monitoring to internet-facing non-production environments. Alert on and investigate any access from non-production systems to production systems, credentials or data. Make application deployment directories read-only for the application runtime user; deploy file-integrity monitoring on application directories for web shell detection. Treat client applications and packages as untrusted: enforce server-side validation of every transaction and business rule; implement API request signing with nonce and timestamp; adopt app attestation services and certificate pinning to detect altered or repackaged applications. Establish a rapid patching SLA for internet-facing applications, prioritizing file-upload and deserialization weaknesses in PHP and Node.js applications; use WAF virtual patching as an interim control. Prohibit hardcoded tokens and credentials in source and build code; deploy automated secret scanning across repositories and CI/CD pipelines; use short-lived, fine-grained, least-privileged access tokens and rotate all build and deployment tokens. Alert on token usage from unusual source IPs, user agents or geographies; enforce branch protection, commit signing and mandatory code review on production deployment branches. Replace IP allow-listing of shared third-party fetcher pools with identity-based controls such as mutual TLS, cryptographically signed requests or scoped API keys on dedicated vendor endpoints. Enforce default-deny egress from server segments through allow-listed proxies; unrestricted HTTPS egress was used for command-and-control and data exfiltration. Deploy TLS inspection with alerting on self-signed certificates presented over non-standard ports. Extend real-time transaction monitoring to flag micro-value test transactions to new beneficiaries followed by high-value transactions; treat this pattern as a strong precursor of unauthorized fund transfer and hold or review such flows. Implement transaction velocity rules, new-beneficiary cooling periods and amount-band anomaly detection across all payment and disbursement paths. Enforce server-side validation, maker-checker approval and reconciliation for all merchant settlement instructions submitted through payment aggregator APIs. Store cryptocurrency wallet keys in hardware security modules or cold custody; require multi-signature approvals for withdrawals; monitor withdrawal patterns for anomalies and rotate keys immediately upon any suspected compromise. Prohibit installation or execution of unauthorized security and attack tools including publicly available AI-driven offensive frameworks on corporate infrastructure; monitor for their download and for AI coding-agent processes running with permission checks disabled. Monitor and govern LLM API usage and keys; LLM API traffic originating from servers or other non-development hosts may indicate an attack rig or planted operator console. Establish a policy requiring written approval, defined scope and a time window for all penetration testing; the tools themselves do not validate authorization. Tune SIEM correlation for machine-speed, multi-technique attack patterns , multiple tools and techniques, parallel attack threads, adaptive payload mutation and continuous non-business-hours operation against a single target and adopt automated (SOAR-based) containment. Deploy deception measures such as honeypots, decoy administrative panels and canary credentials; autonomous attack agents enumerate targets exhaustively and are likely to touch decoy assets, generating high-confidence early alerts. Monitor web roots, temporary directories and staging paths for bursts of newly created commented scripts and rapid successive variants of functionally identical scripts - a strong indicator of AI-generated attack tooling. Adopt zero-trust principles , micro-segmentation, identity-based access for every user and service, and inspection of east-west traffic operating on the assumption that the threat actor is already inside the environment. Upon detection of suspicious activity: isolate affected hosts, preserve forensic evidence and logs, rotate all credentials, and report to CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin at incident@cert-in.org.in . Conclusion Entities are advised to report any signs of suspicious activity related to the "CRAFTY FALCON" campaign to CERT-In/CSIRT-Fin at incident@cert-in.org.in , along with all relevant logs, at the earliest. Entities shall also contact Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C) for reporting of such fraudulent transactions in bulk at Cyber Fraud Mitigation Centre (CFCFRMS Portal). The detailed (restricted) version of this advisory, including the full indicators of compromise, infrastructure fingerprints and detection rules, has been shared with BFSI entities at the appropriate TLP level. Indicators may change while adversary techniques often remain consistent; entities should therefore not limit their response to blocking indicators.

artifact.author: Graham Hill
artifact.literal_explanation_frozen: Previously trusted access stops being reliable evidence of legitimate action when an attacker can reuse an accepted credential or originate requests through an accepted infrastructure path, and the receiving system accepts that access without independently establishing authorization for the specific action. The recurring relationship is that an access signal can remain valid after control of its use has changed. This is a bounded inference from Cloudflare’s incident account and CERT-In’s reporting chain; it does not imply that every trusted access path is compromised or that every compromise permits unrestricted action.

editorial.title: Valid access. Unauthorized action.
editorial.body:
A credential can still work after it has been stolen. That makes successful authentication a limited answer to a much bigger business question: should this action happen?

Cloudflare reports that one service token and three accounts associated with credentials stolen in the October 2023 Okta compromise were left unrotated after being mistakenly considered unused. Attackers later used those credentials to access its Atlassian environment. Cloudflare also reports that segmentation and other controls limited lateral movement, with no customer data or global network changes affected. [CF2024]

In a separate reporting chain, CERT-In describes attackers using stolen payment credentials to invoke fund-transfer APIs from victims’ own whitelisted infrastructure. Those requests bypassed application checks including sanction, beneficiary verification and balance sufficiency. [CIAD-2026-0046]

CERT-In’s subsequent update describes another way an accepted origin could mislead: requests arriving through whitelisted third-party fetcher pools that Internet users could cause to fetch arbitrary URLs. This update belongs to the same reporting chain, not a third independent confirmation. [CIAD-2026-0058]

The inference is narrow but consequential: a valid credential or accepted network origin cannot, by itself, establish that the current operator or requested action is authorized. Its technical validity can outlast the conditions that made it trustworthy.

For leaders, the practical question is where authorization for the actual business action gets checked. CERT-In recommends validating payouts against approved records and binding transaction stages so a debit cannot skip preceding validation. Those are recommendations, not measured proof of effectiveness. [CIAD-2026-0046]

Access is evidence. The decision is how much it proves.

claim_support.claim: Unrotated stolen credentials enabled later access to Cloudflare’s Atlassian environment.
Segmentation and other controls limited lateral movement; Cloudflare reported no customer data or global network changes affected.
Attackers invoked payment APIs using valid stolen credentials from victims’ whitelisted infrastructure, bypassing application-level checks.
Shared third-party fetcher pools allowed attacker-induced requests to originate from whitelisted IPs.
An accepted access signal can remain valid after an attacker gains control of its use, so it is insufficient alone to establish authorization for a specific action.
claim_support.reasoning: The independent Cloudflare and CERT-In accounts describe attacker use of credentials or origins still accepted by target systems. The CERT-In update extends the mechanism within that same reporting chain.

claim_support.claim: CERT-In recommends approved-record validation and cryptographic binding of transaction stages.
claim_support.qualification: The supplied material does not measure these recommendations’ effectiveness.

limitations: Analysis uses only the supplied source material; source authenticity and full context were not independently verified.
There are two independent reporting origins, not three: CIAD-2026-0058 explicitly updates CIAD-2026-0046.

Cloudflare’s retrospective account and CERT-In’s financial-sector reporting concern different organizations, periods and systems. They support a conceptual relationship, not a shared attacker, identical failure or universal outcome.
Cloudflare’s reported containment bounds the argument: compromised access does not necessarily enable unrestricted lateral movement or downstream damage.
No causal claim about AI is needed or established by this comparison.
No hypothetical incident, personal experience, motive or invented quotation is used. The literal explanation precedes the editorial, and no imagery is proposed.

style_traits.rhythm: Short hooks, varied sentence length, compact paragraphs and occasional one-line punches.
style_traits.reasoning: Challenge a supported assumption; connect the mechanism to earned practical or human stakes.
style_traits.imagery: Vivid but controlled; use analogy or dry humour only when useful. No invented incidents or dramatic outcomes.

artifact.author: Graham Hill
artifact.title: The key still works. What does that prove?
artifact.literal_explanation: Previously trusted access stops being reliable evidence of legitimate action when an attacker can reuse an accepted credential or originate requests through an accepted infrastructure path, and the receiving system accepts that access without independently establishing authorization for the specific action. An access signal can remain valid after control of its use has changed. This is a bounded inference, not evidence that every trusted path is compromised or that compromised access permits unrestricted action.

reported_facts.text: Cloudflare reports that one service token and three accounts associated with stolen credentials were left unrotated and later used by attackers to access its Atlassian environment. It also reports that segmentation and other controls limited lateral movement, with no customer data or global network changes affected.
CERT-In reports attackers invoking fund-transfer APIs using stolen credentials from victims’ whitelisted infrastructure, bypassing application-level business checks.

CERT-In’s subsequent update reports abuse of whitelisted third-party fetcher pools through which Internet users could induce requests. This is part of the same reporting chain as the earlier advisory.

artifact.inference: A valid credential or accepted origin is insufficient by itself to establish authorization for the current action.

hypothetical_illustrations.image: A working office key establishes that a lock can be opened; it does not establish permission to remove the equipment inside.
hypothetical_illustrations.classification: Hypothetical analogy, not a reported event.

mapping.evidence: Cloudflare’s stolen credentials remained usable after being left unrotated.
Attackers subsequently accessed Cloudflare’s Atlassian environment.
Conceptual counterpart to authorization for a specific business action; CERT-In reports payment requests bypassing application checks.
Cloudflare reports segmentation and other controls limiting lateral movement.

hypothetical_illustrations.where_it_breaks: Digital credentials can be copied and used remotely. A physical key does not represent shared network origins or transaction-stage validation. Removing equipment is illustrative, not an allegation about Cloudflare.

hypothetical_illustrations.image: A familiar courier arriving at the loading bay does not establish that every parcel has an approved purchase order.
hypothetical_illustrations.classification: Hypothetical analogy, not a reported event.

mapping.evidence: CERT-In describes requests arriving through whitelisted third-party fetcher IP pools.
CERT-In states that Internet users could cause those shared fetcher services to request arbitrary URLs.
Conceptual counterpart to CERT-In’s recommendation to validate payouts against sanctioned or approved records.

hypothetical_illustrations.where_it_breaks: Fetching a URL is not delivering a physical parcel. The comparison does not establish that a fetcher alone can authorize or execute a payout; other credentials and endpoint conditions may matter.

hypothetical_illustrations.image: A staff badge that opens the building is not approval to pay an invoice.
hypothetical_illustrations.classification: Hypothetical analogy, not a reported event.

mapping.evidence: Conceptual counterpart to the valid stolen credentials described by Cloudflare and CERT-In.

mapping.part: Entry being confused with payment approval
mapping.evidence: CERT-In reports direct fund-transfer API invocation bypassing application-level checks, including sanction and beneficiary verification.
Conceptual counterpart to CERT-In’s recommendations for approved-record validation and maker-checker verification.

hypothetical_illustrations.where_it_breaks: Building entry and invoice approval are visibly separate processes; an API credential may itself carry payment privileges. The analogy cannot establish that these systems literally confused a login with approval or lacked every authorization control.

selected_analogy.reason: The physical-versus-digital differences do not change the central conclusion: continued acceptance of an access mechanism does not establish the holder’s authority for a subsequent action. The additional locked-room comparison also preserves the evidence that compromised access can remain contained.

outline.image: The key still turns. That tells you something about the lock—and only so much about the person holding it.
outline.real_mechanism: Cloudflare reports attacker use of unrotated stolen credentials, alongside effective limits on lateral movement. Separately, CERT-In reports stolen credentials and accepted infrastructure paths supporting unauthorized payment API calls. [CF2024; CIAD-2026-0046; CIAD-2026-0058]
outline.boundary: This is an analogy about the limits of access evidence. It does not equate the incidents, establish a shared attacker, or imply unrestricted damage. Digital credentials and network paths do not behave exactly like physical keys.
outline.action: Ask where each fund movement is checked against an approved business record and whether the debit can bypass prior validation. CERT-In recommends approved-record validation and cryptographic binding of transaction stages; the supplied evidence does not measure their effectiveness. [CIAD-2026-0046]

claim_support.claim: Unrotated stolen credentials enabled later access to Cloudflare’s Atlassian environment.
Segmentation and other controls limited lateral movement, with no customer data or global network changes affected.
Attackers used stolen credentials from whitelisted infrastructure to invoke payment APIs and bypass application-level business checks.
Shared fetcher services enabled attacker-induced requests from whitelisted IP pools.
An accepted credential or origin alone cannot establish authorization for a specific action after an attacker gains control of its use.
claim_support.reasoning: Two independent reporting origins describe attacker use of signals that target systems continued to accept; the later CERT-In advisory extends its existing reporting chain.

claim_support.claim: CERT-In recommends approved-record validation, maker-checker verification and cryptographic binding of transaction stages.
claim_support.qualification: Recommendations are not measured evidence of effectiveness.

claim_support.claim: The key, courier and badge situations illustrate the distinction between accepted access and authorized action.
claim_support.qualification: These are explanatory comparisons, not additional incidents or independent evidence.

limitations: Only supplied material was used; source authenticity and full context were not independently verified.
There are two independent reporting origins, not three: the November CERT-In advisory updates the October advisory.
The accounts concern different organizations, periods and systems; the comparison supports a conceptual relationship, not a shared attacker or identical failure.
Cloudflare’s reported containment rules out treating compromised access as proof of unrestricted downstream impact.
No causal claim about AI is needed or established.
Analogy mappings do not add factual evidence or demonstrate control effectiveness.
